Lantern Ledger marks a payment as paid and publishes a notification for its identifier. Originally, both awaited operations ran inside the database transaction callback. The database commits staged writes only after that callback fulfills, so publication happened before commit.

The notification is external to the transaction. Putting publish(id) inside the callback makes the database wait for it, but cannot make a rollback retract it.

" 33: }, 34: { 35: "pointer": "/sections/1/eyebrow", 36: "value": "The gap" 37: }, 38: { 39: "pointer": "/sections/1/title", 40: "value": "A notification could outlive a rollback" 41: }, 42: { 43: "pointer": "/sections/1/content", 44: "value": "

A failed commit could leave you with a notification for an unpaid record. The supplied probe demonstrates this: the original function publishes once, then rolls back when commit fails. Publication can also become visible before its own promise rejects, triggering a rollback after the notification escapes.

The author describes the change as making payment and notification atomic. The source supports a narrower guarantee: it orders publication after a successful commit. These operations still cannot succeed or fail as one unit.

" 45: }, 46: { 47: "pointer": "/sections/2/eyebrow", 48: "value": "The changed mechanism" 49: }, 50: { 51: "pointer": "/sections/2/title", 52: "value": "Wait for the transaction, then publish" 53: }, 54: { 55: "pointer": "/sections/2/content", 56: "value": "

The changed function first awaits the transaction itself:

{{CODE:0}}

That promise fulfills only after commit. A write or commit rejection therefore exits the function before publication. The next statement runs outside the callback:

{{CODE:1}}

Publication failure now leaves the payment committed. In the supplied results, rejection before visibility leaves zero notifications; rejection after visibility leaves one. Both calls report an error, so an error alone cannot tell you whether delivery occurred.

The probe models staged writes and an external counter, rather than a real database. Its assertions cover ordering and these failure outcomes; it does not simulate a process stopping.

" 57: }, 58: { 59: "pointer": "/sections/3/eyebrow", 60: "value": "The short version" 61: }, 62: { 63: "pointer": "/sections/3/title", 64: "value": "Safer ordering, separate delivery" 65: }, 66: { 67: "pointer": "/sections/3/content", 68: "value": "

Failed transactions no longer reach publication. Delivery remains vulnerable to a process stopping between commit and publish, with no durable outbox or background retry supplied. Retrying after a visible notification can duplicate it. An idempotent markPaid does not deduplicate publication: the probe's two concurrent calls produce two notifications in both versions. This change fixes premature notification, not atomic or exactly-once delivery.

" 69: } 70: ]

3:   "body": "The author says moving publish prevents notifications for failed commits and makes payment and notification atomic.",
4:   "contracts": [
5:     "transaction invokes the callback once and commits its staged writes only after callback fulfillment. It fulfills with undefined after commit. Callback or commit rejection rolls back all staged writes.",
6:     "publish is an external operation outside the database transaction. Its rejection may happen before or after an externally visible notification.",
7:     "markPaid is idempotent for a given id. Neither transaction nor publish supplies a delivery deduplication guarantee.",
8:     "A process can stop between awaited operations. No durable outbox, background retry, or cross-call lock is supplied."
9:   ],
10:   "before": "export async function before(db, publish, id) {\n  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {\n    await tx.markPaid(id);\n    await publish(id);\n  });\n}",
11:   "after": "export async function after(db, publish, id) {\n  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {\n    await tx.markPaid(id);\n  });\n  await publish(id);\n}",
12:   "unchanged": "none"
13: }

input.command: node --input-type=module -e 'import fs from "node:fs"; import crypto from "node:crypto"; import assert from "node:assert/strict"; const raw = fs.readFileSync("manifest.json"); const manifest = JSON.parse(raw); const fields = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("fields.json", "utf8")); const audit = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("audit.json", "utf8")); assert.equal(crypto.createHash("sha256").update(raw).digest("hex"), audit.inputSha256); assert.deepEqual(audit.reviewedPointers, fields.map(f => f.pointer)); assert.equal(new Set(audit.reviewedPointers).size, fields.length); for (const f of fields) assert.equal(f.pointer.slice(1).split("/").reduce((o,k) => o[k], manifest), f.value); assert.equal(audit.verdict, "pass"); for (const key of ["findings", "edits", "blockers"]) assert.deepEqual(audit[key], []); console.log("Verified manifest hash, all 17 text fields, and pass audit structure.");'
